theme: Israel’s persistent adultery; “How can I give you up?”
readingInstruction: Read Hosea 8:1-11:12. Chapters 8 to 10 describe Israel’s idolatry and coming judgment. Chapter 11 is one of the most emotionally powerful chapters in the prophets: God’s heart breaks over his people. Read chapter 11 slowly.
settingTheScene: These chapters continue the lawsuit against Israel. The people have made kings without God’s approval, set up idols, and made alliances with Assyria. They will reap what they sow. But in chapter 11, the language changes from a courtroom to a family. God is a father who taught his child to walk, and the child went away. The chapter is among the clearest statements in the Old Testament of God’s compassionate heart.
observation: “For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (8:7).
“For Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces” (8:14).
“Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you” (10:12).
“You have plowed iniquity; you have reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies” (10:13).
“When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son” (11:1).
“Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms, but they did not know that I healed them” (11:3).
“I led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love” (11:4).
“How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel?… My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender” (11:8).
interpretation:
The sayings of chapters 8 to 10 contain some of the most quoted lines in Hosea. “They sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.” Sin has consequences that exceed what we expect. A small seed of rebellion grows into a storm. “Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces.” The root of the problem is forgetting God, and the result is a grand life built without him.

Chapter 10 contains a call that is both an accusation and an invitation: “Break up your fallow ground.” Fallow ground is hard, unplowed soil. The people’s hearts have become hard. God invites them to cultivate them, to sow righteousness and reap steadfast love, to seek the LORD until he rains righteousness on them. Even in judgment, there is an open door.

Chapter 11 is the emotional center of the book. God remembers when Israel was a child. “Out of Egypt I called my son.” He taught him to walk, held him by the arms, healed him, and led him with cords of kindness. The picture of a parent teaching a toddler to take steps is touching. But the more they were called, the more they went away. They sacrificed to Baals and offered incense to idols. Now they will go into exile.

Then God asks, “How can I give you up, O Ephraim?” The sentence is a cry from the heart. Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed along with Sodom. God says, “How can I make you like Admah?” His heart recoils. “My compassion grows warm and tender.” God does not simply carry out judgment. He struggles with it. The text shows his holiness and his love in tension, and love wins: “I will not execute my burning anger… for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst.”

This is a deep statement of who God is. His love is not like human love, which gives up when it is wounded. He is God, and he will not give up.
connection: Matthew 2:15 quotes Hosea 11:1 and applies it to Jesus, who was called out of Egypt as God’s true Son, the faithful Israel. Jesus wept over Jerusalem as a hen gathering her chicks (Matthew 23:37). Jesus is the one in whom God’s compassion took flesh. Luke 15:20 shows the father running to the prodigal son. 1 John 4:10 says, “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us.”
application:
Ask where you have “fallow ground,” areas where your heart has hardened. Begin to break it up.

Take comfort from the image of God teaching you to walk. Where has he held you by the arms without your noticing?

Reflect on “How can I give you up?” and let it settle in your heart.
prayerPrompts: Confess what you have sown and fear to reap.
Ask him to break up the fallow ground of your heart.
Thank him for teaching you to walk and leading you with cords of kindness.
